steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (PACE) is the primary statute governing police powers in England and Wales, balancing effective law enforcement with the protection of individual rights

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Stop and search under PACE section 1 requires reasonable suspicion that the person has stolen or prohibited articles; the officer must state their name, station and the grounds for the search

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Reasonable suspicion must be based on objective factors — it cannot be based solely on a person's race, age or appearance (PACE Code A)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: An arrest without warrant under PACE section 24 requires reasonable suspicion that the person is about to commit, is committing or has committed an offence, and the arrest must be necessary

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always link police powers back to the PACE 1984 and cite specific sections where possible (e.g. section 1 for stop and search, section 24 for arrest) When evaluating police powers, present both sides: effective law enforcement versus protection of civil liberties Use statistical evidence on stop and search disproportionality to support arguments about civil liberties concerns Remember the modified right to silence — candidates often forget the 1994 Act allows adverse inferences When discussing detention time limits, distinguish between the 24-hour, 36-hour and 96-hour limits and who can authorise each extension
